title: Minimum Path Sum
directAnswer: Let dp[i][j] be the cheapest path sum from the top-left to cell (i, j) moving only right or down. Then dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]), with the first row and column as running prefix sums. Naive recursion is exponential; the DP is O(mn) time, O(mn) space, and compresses to a single O(n) rolling row.

remember.pattern: 2D grid DP — cheapest path, right/down only
remember.formula:
dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
first row: dp[0][j] = dp[0][j-1] + grid[0][j]
first col: dp[i][0] = dp[i-1][0] + grid[i][0]
rules: You may move only **right or down**, so a cell is reached only from its **top or left** neighbour — that's why the recurrence has exactly two terms.
Always **add** the current cell's value `grid[i][j]`; the choice is which cheaper predecessor to extend.
The first row and first column have only **one** way in (straight from the start), so they're plain **prefix sums** — get these base cases right or the interior is garbage.
Take the **min** of the two predecessors (this is optimization), not the sum — a classic mix-up with counting DPs like Unique Paths.
Each cell reads only the row above and the cell to its left, so the whole table collapses to **one rolling row** of length n → O(n) space.
whenToUse: Cheapest / longest path through a grid with restricted moves (right/down)
Each cell's optimum depends only on a couple of neighbouring cells
Accumulating a cost while moving monotonically through a matrix
Counting or optimizing over lattice paths
antiSignals: Moves in all four directions with arbitrary weights → Dijkstra / 0-1 BFS, not simple DP
You need every path, not the best one → enumerate / backtrack
Counting the number of paths, not their cost → Unique Paths (sum, not min)
Negative cycles or revisiting cells allowed → shortest-path graph algorithms
remember.takeaway: Minimum Path Sum is the cleanest 'cheapest monotone path on a grid' DP: each cell is its own cost plus the cheaper of the two ways in. Once you see it, Unique Paths (count instead of min), Triangle, and Dungeon Game are the same grid recurrence with different operators and directions.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that right/down-only movement forces a two-term recurrence (top or left), handle the first row/column base cases, and know to MIN over predecessors while ADDING the current cell.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting the first row/column are prefix sums (treating their missing neighbours as 0 cost), or summing the two predecessors instead of taking the min.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the recurrence from 'a cell is reachable only from top or left', handle the borders explicitly, then compress to a single O(n) row updated in place.

problemStatement:
Given a `m x n` `grid` filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from the **top-left** to the **bottom-right** which ***minimizes the sum*** of all numbers along its path.

You can only move either **down** or **right** at any point in time.
understanding: Walk from the upper-left cell to the lower-right cell, stepping only right or down, and minimize the total of the values you land on (both endpoints included). All values are non-negative, so there's no incentive to wander — the only question is which mix of right/down moves is cheapest.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which moves are allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only right and down. That monotonic restriction is what makes a simple two-term DP work instead of a full shortest-path search.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the cell values always non-negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, 0 to 200. Non-negativity means greedy detours never help, but we still need DP because local minima don't guarantee a global minimum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do both endpoints count toward the sum?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the path includes the starting cell and the destination cell, so the start's value is added once at the base case.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the grid be a single row or column?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Then there's exactly one path — the prefix sum of that row/column — which the base-case handling covers directly.

examples.explanation: The path 1→3→1→1→1 (right, right, down, down) sums to 7, the minimum.
Single cell — start equals destination, sum is just its value.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. Minimum Path Sum lands on the rolling-row grid-DP branch.

diagrams.title: Each cell is reached from top or left only
diagrams.caption: Right/down moves mean (i, j) has exactly two predecessors. Extend the cheaper one and add the current value.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recurse Both Moves
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this to establish the recurrence, then flag the exponential path explosion before switching to a table.
hints: From any cell you can go right or down. The cheapest path from here to the goal is this cell's value plus the cheaper of those two continuations.
Write cost(i, j) = grid[i][j] + min(cost(i+1, j), cost(i, j+1)), recursing toward the bottom-right.
Base case: the destination cell returns its own value; stepping off the grid returns +infinity so it's never chosen.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each call branches into two (right and down), and a path is m+n−2 moves long, so the recursion tree has up to ~2^(m+n) nodes. Stack depth is O(m+n).
approaches.explanation:
Translate the movement rules directly: from cell `(i, j)` you may step right to `(i, j+1)` or down to `(i+1, j)`. The cheapest cost to finish from `(i, j)` is `grid[i][j]` plus the smaller of the two recursive continuations.

**Why this is the honest first attempt.** The problem is literally 'choose right or down at each step to minimize the total'. The recursion makes that choice explicit at every cell and lets `min` pick the better branch. No insight about reuse is needed yet — just exhaustive choice.

**Why the base cases are what they are.** At the bottom-right cell there's nothing left to do, so it returns its own value. Stepping past the last row or column is illegal; modeling that as `+infinity` guarantees `min` never selects an off-grid move, so we don't need special boundary branches sprinkled through the logic.

**Why we don't ship this.** Two length-200 sides give paths of ~400 moves and a recursion tree near `2^400` — utterly intractable. Crucially, the same cell `(i, j)` is reached by exponentially many different prefixes, and each time we recompute `cost(i, j)` from scratch. That overlap — identical subproblems revisited — is the unmistakable cue to memoize, then tabulate.
approaches.insight: Different prefixes converge on the same cell, and the cost *from* that cell onward doesn't depend on how you arrived — only on where you are. That 'future is independent of the past given the current state' property is exactly what lets caching collapse the exponential path count into one value per cell.

dryRun.intro: cost(i, j) = grid[i][j] + min(down, right). Off-grid returns +inf so it's never picked.

java.explanation: Off-grid is illegal — return MAX_VALUE so min() never walks off the board.
Destination cell: nothing left to add, just its own value.
Pay this cell, then extend the cheaper of the two legal moves. This line IS the algorithm.

python.explanation: Out of bounds → infinity, never selected by min.

python.line: if i == m - 1 and j == n - 1:
python.explanation: Goal reached — return the cell value alone.

python.line: return grid[i][j] + min(cost(i + 1, j), cost(i, j + 1))
python.explanation: Current cost plus the cheaper continuation.

edgeCases.behavior: Start equals destination → the base case returns 5 immediately.
Down is always off-grid (inf), so the path is forced right: 1+2+3 = 6.

pitfalls: Returning 0 for off-grid instead of +infinity — lets min pick an illegal move and undercounts.
Summing the two continuations instead of taking the min — counts both branches.
Shipping the recursion — exponential and hopeless for 200×200 grids.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up 2D DP — Cell + min(Top, Left)
approaches.whenToMention: The clean tabulated form. Lead with 'dp[i][j] = cheapest sum to REACH (i, j) from the start', filling forward from the top-left.
hints: Flip the direction: instead of cost-to-finish from a cell, compute cost-to-REACH each cell from the top-left. Then dp[m-1][n-1] is the answer.
A cell is entered only from above or from the left, so dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
Seed the borders: dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]; the first row and first column are running prefix sums since each has just one way in.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every cell is filled once with O(1) work over an m×n grid → O(mn) time. The dp table stores one value per cell → O(mn) space.
approaches.explanation:
Define `dp[i][j]` as the minimum sum of any right/down path from the start `(0, 0)` to cell `(i, j)`. Because movement is monotone, `(i, j)` can only be entered from directly above or directly to the left, so its best cost is its own value plus the cheaper of those two predecessors.

**Why the borders are prefix sums.** The top-left cell has no predecessor, so `dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]`. Any cell in the first row can only be reached by moving right along that row — a single forced path — so `dp[0][j] = dp[0][j-1] + grid[0][j]`. Likewise the first column is reached only by moving down: `dp[i][0] = dp[i-1][0] + grid[i][0]`. Skipping these and pretending a missing neighbour costs 0 would let interior cells 'inherit' a free path that doesn't exist.

**Why min, and why we still add the cell.** This is an optimization, not a count: among the (at most two) ways to arrive, we keep the cheaper, hence `min`. But every path that ends at `(i, j)` must stand on `(i, j)`, so its value is always added. Confusing this with Unique Paths — where you *sum* the two predecessors to *count* routes — is the classic trap.

**Why a row-major fill is a valid order.** Each `dp[i][j]` depends only on `dp[i-1][j]` (the row above, already done) and `dp[i][j-1]` (the same row, already done to the left). Scanning top-to-bottom, left-to-right therefore always has both dependencies ready. The answer is the bottom-right cell, `dp[m-1][n-1]`.
approaches.insight: Reframing from 'cheapest cost to finish from here' (top-down) to 'cheapest cost to reach here' (bottom-up) is what removes the recursion: dependencies now point backward to already-filled cells, so a plain double loop suffices. That reframe — define the state as 'best value ending at this cell' — is the workhorse of nearly every grid DP.

dryRun.intro: dp[i][j] = cheapest sum to reach (i, j). Borders are prefix sums; interior takes cell + min(top, left).

java.explanation: Start cell's value is included once — the seed of the whole table.
First row has a single way in (from the left), so it's a running prefix sum.
First column is reached only from above — another prefix sum.
Interior: own value plus the cheaper of top and left. Add the cell, MIN the predecessors.

python.explanation: First-row prefix sums — only one path along the top.
Cell cost + cheaper predecessor; min because we optimize, + because the cell is always on the path.

edgeCases.behavior: m = 1: only the first-row prefix-sum loop runs → dp = [1,3,6], answer 6.
n = 1: only the first-column loop runs → dp = [1,3,6], answer 6.

pitfalls: Forgetting to seed the first row/column — interior cells then read uninitialized 0s and undercount.
Summing dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] instead of taking the min — that counts paths (Unique Paths), not the cheapest cost.
Returning dp[0][0] or a tracked min instead of dp[m-1][n-1] — the answer is specifically the destination cell.

approaches.name: Space-Optimized — Single Rolling Row (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The polish: 'each cell only needs the row above and the cell to its left, so one row of length n is enough'.
hints: Look at the 2D recurrence: dp[i][j] reads dp[i-1][j] (the row above) and dp[i][j-1] (this row, already updated). Do you need all m rows in memory?
Keep one array of length n. Initialize it to the first row's prefix sums, then for each later row update it left to right in place.
When you reach index j, dp[j] still holds the value from the row above (the top), and dp[j-1] already holds this row's left — so dp[j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j-1]).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Same O(mn) cell updates with O(1) work each. Storage is a single array of n values regardless of m → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The 2D recurrence never reaches further back than one row, so we can keep just **one array** `dp` of length `n` and overwrite it as we descend the grid. Before processing row `i`, `dp` holds row `i-1`; after the inner loop, it holds row `i`.

**Why a single row is exact.** When the inner loop reaches column `j`, two facts hold simultaneously: `dp[j]` has *not yet* been overwritten this row, so it still equals `dp[i-1][j]` — the value from directly above (the top). And `dp[j-1]` *was* just updated, so it equals `dp[i][j-1]` — this row's left neighbour. Those are precisely the two predecessors the full table reads. So `dp[j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j-1])` reproduces the 2D recurrence with no information lost.

**Handling the borders in the rolled form.** Initialize `dp` to the first row's prefix sums. For each subsequent row, the leftmost cell `dp[0]` has no left neighbour, so it just accumulates downward: `dp[0] += grid[i][0]`. Then the inner loop runs from `j = 1`. Unlike the saved-diagonal trick in Edit Distance or Maximal Square, this recurrence only needs the top and the left — never the diagonal — so no `prev`/`temp` stash is required, which makes it the simplest of the rolling-row DPs.

**Why the left-to-right order is mandatory.** We must read `dp[j]` as the top *before* overwriting it, and `dp[j-1]` must already be this row's value. Sweeping left to right satisfies both: each cell is updated exactly when its top is still stale and its left is already fresh. Reverse the direction and `dp[j-1]` would still be the old row, corrupting the recurrence.
approaches.insight: When a grid recurrence depends only on the row above and the cell immediately left, a single row updated left-to-right is all the memory you need — and because there's no diagonal term, this one needs no saved-corner scalar at all. Recognizing exactly which neighbours a recurrence touches tells you precisely how much state to keep.

Leftmost cell of each new row has no left neighbour, so it only accumulates the value above it.
dp[j] is still the TOP (not yet overwritten), dp[j-1] is the LEFT (already updated this row) — exactly the two predecessors.

Update column-0 base case for the current row.
min of stale-top dp[j] and fresh-left dp[j-1]; left-to-right order keeps both correct.

diagrams.title: The single row morphing per grid row
diagrams.caption: dp starts as the top row's prefix sums, then each grid row rewrites it left to right.

edgeCases.behavior: Only the init loop runs; dp ends as the row's prefix sums, returning the last entry.
n = 1, the inner loop never runs; dp[0] accumulates every row's value → the column total.

pitfalls: Iterating the inner loop right-to-left — dp[j-1] would still be the previous row, breaking the recurrence.
Forgetting dp[0] += grid[i][0] each row — the first column loses its accumulated cost.
Re-initializing dp inside the row loop — wipes out the row-above values you need as the 'top'.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the first row and first column are prefix sums — they have only one way in.
Summing the two predecessors instead of taking the min — that counts paths instead of minimizing cost.
Returning a cell other than the bottom-right — the answer is specifically dp[m-1][n-1].

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Min vs sum of predecessors
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Minimum Path Sum OPTIMIZES a cost, so you keep the cheaper predecessor. Summing them solves Unique Paths (counting routes) instead and returns a wildly inflated number.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Unseeded borders
commonMistakesDetailed.why: First-row and first-column cells have a single predecessor. Leaving them at 0 lets interior cells read a phantom free path from off the grid.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(m)]
# jump straight to the interior double loop

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong sweep direction in the rolled row
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The O(n) version needs dp[j-1] to already hold the CURRENT row's left value. Iterating right-to-left leaves dp[j-1] as the previous row, silently producing wrong sums.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for j in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
    dp[j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j - 1])
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for j in range(1, n):
    dp[j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j - 1])

followupVariations.hint: Same cheapest-path idea on a triangular grid; bottom-up DP runs in O(n) space.

followupVariations.title: Dungeon Game
followupVariations.hint: Same grid moves but DP runs bottom-right to top-left and tracks minimum health needed, not accumulated sum.

patternNote: Canonical 'cheapest monotone path on a grid' DP. Recognize it whenever moves are restricted to right/down (or any monotone direction) and you optimize an accumulated cost. The same recurrence underpins Unique Paths (sum to count), Triangle, and — reversed — Dungeon Game.
